outline.description: Sets out who the parties are, what happened on the Cameo platform, how the videos were used on Jimmy Kimmel Live!, and how the case reached the Second Circuit, including the applicable standard of review and materials the court could consider on a Rule 12(b)(6) motion.
subtopics: Parties: George Santos (plaintiff-appellant) vs. Jimmy Kimmel, ABC, The Walt Disney Company (defendants-appellees)
Factual core: Kimmel’s use of fictitious names to purchase Santos Cameo videos; broadcast in the “Will Santos Say It?” segments on JKL
Claims: Copyright infringement plus state-law claims (breach of contract, breach of implied contract, fraudulent inducement)
District Court ruling: Dismissal under Rule 12(b)(6); copyright claims barred by fair use; state claims preempted or failed to state a claim
Standard of review: De novo review of 12(b)(6) dismissals; considering complaint, attached exhibits, incorporated documents
Judicial notice: Copyright Office registrations as noticed materials
Appellate framing: Whether fair use is established on the pleadings; whether state-law theories state a claim (without resolving preemption)

outline.chapter_title: Fair Use Framework and Pleading-Stage Adjudication
outline.description: Explains the legal standards governing fair use under 17 U.S.C. § 107, the focus on transformative purpose, and why the Second Circuit can resolve fair use on a motion to dismiss based on the complaint and the works themselves.
subtopics: Fair use as an affirmative defense that furthers copyright’s goals
Section 107 factors: purpose and character; nature of work; amount and substantiality; market effect
Transformative use inquiry: reasonable observer standard vs. subjective intent (Warhol v. Goldsmith, 598 U.S. 508)
Flexibility of fair use and context-specific analysis
Pleading-stage resolution: when fair use is clear from the complaint and the works (TCA Television; Cariou v. Prince)
Permissible record: Original Cameo videos and JKL segments; copyright registrations

outline.chapter_title: Applying the Fair Use Factors to Kimmel’s Broadcasts
outline.description: Details the court’s analysis of each fair use factor, including transformation, publication status, amount used, and market harm, as well as Santos’s bad-faith argument.
subtopics: Purpose and character: JKL’s commentary on Santos’s willingness to say absurd things for money; distinct purpose from original videos’ conveyed messages of hope/encouragement
Objective lens: Reasonable observer, not Santos’s or Kimmel’s subjective intent; rejection of the claim that Kimmel “designed” the original purpose by prompting the lines
Bad faith argument: Harper & Row’s good-faith dictum narrowed; complaint shows criticism/commentary, not intent to supplant Santos’s rights
Nature of the work: Videos were published the day they were created per registrations; implications for factor two
Amount and substantiality: Use tied to the commentary purpose in a comedic critique segment
Market effect: No usurpation of the market for the original videos; criticism and lampooning are outside potential licensing markets (Campbell; Hachette Book Group)
Bottom line: First factor strongly favors fair use; remaining factors do not show market substitution; fair use established on the pleadings

outline.chapter_title: State Law Claims: Contract Theories and Fraud
outline.description: Explores why the court affirms dismissal of Santos’s state-law claims without resolving preemption: failure to plead a viable third-party beneficiary claim under Illinois law, an implied-in-fact contract under New York law, or out-of-pocket loss for fraudulent inducement.
subtopics: Preemption posture: Court bypasses preemption and affirms on failure-to-state-a-claim grounds

Direct breach of contract (Cameo Terms of Service; Illinois law): Strong presumption against third-party beneficiaries; need for practically express declaration; no provision extending enforceable rights to Santos

Implied-in-fact contract (New York law): Requirement to plead essential terms and a meeting of the minds; complaint’s conclusory allegations; no plausible agreement that Kimmel would adhere to Cameo’s Terms
Fraudulent inducement (New York law): Out-of-pocket loss rule (Lama Holding; Connaughton); failure to allege actual pecuniary loss caused by the alleged misrepresentations
Disposition: All state claims properly dismissed for failure to state a claim

outline.description: Summarizes the court’s ultimate decision and its instructional value on transformative fair use in comedic commentary and the limits of contract and fraud theories tied to platform terms.
subtopics: Holding: Affirmance of dismissal; fair use bars copyright claims; state-law claims fail on their elements
Disposition: Judgment of the District Court affirmed
Key takeaways on fair use: Objective purpose controls; comedic commentary and critique can be transformative even where the defendant instigates content
Market-harm clarification: Criticism/lampooning does not create a cognizable licensing market for the plaintiff
Contract lessons: Third-party beneficiary hurdles under Illinois law; specificity and mutual assent required for implied contracts under New York law
Fraud lesson: Necessity of pleading actual out-of-pocket loss, not reputational or expectancy harms
